extracted.intended_audience: scholars, editors, and students of textual criticism, classical mathematics, and the transmission/edition of Archimedes (historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evidential criteria for establishing the relationships, dating, and trustworthiness of Greek manuscripts and their Latin translations (specifically for Archimedes' works) by comparing provenance notes, palaeography, contents, lacunae, translations and editorial practice. Useful for editors preparing critical editions or historians reconstructing transmission history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and ownership-notes as dating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ownership names and documentary notes in a copy (e.g. that the archetype belonged to George Valla and afterwards to Albertus Pius) to infer dates and copying relationships (e.g. B written before Albertus’ death in 1531 because Rodolphus Pius is not mentioned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from text: absence/presence of an owner's name (Rodolphus Pius) lets one infer relative chronology. Look for letters, dedications, or notes stating for whom/when a copy was made (e.g. C made by Christophorus Auverus in 1544 for Georgius Armagniacus). Treat such documentary evidence as strong external corroboration of a manuscript's origin when consistent with other data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of peculiar abbreviations and orthographic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of peculiar abbreviations used in an archetype are important for comparison with other manuscripts and for establishing common origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note to B gives a list of peculiar abbreviations which ‘is of importance for the purpose of comparison with F and other MSS.’ Collate abbreviation-forms and contraction conventions across witnesses; consistent idiosyncratic abbreviations strongly indicate descent from the same archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical condition and shared lacunae as transmission evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubbing/worn first or last pages, missing folios, and the same lacunae occurring in multiple MSS indicate they derive from a common illegible archetype or share a damaged exemplar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: C’s preface states the first page of the archetype was so rubbed that Archimedes’ name could not be read; F, B show corresponding deficiencies. A lacuna at a particular location (p.4 of Vol. iii) appearing in all three MSS supports common ancestry. Note also copyist remarks about missing pages (e.g. B’s scribe notes one or two pages missing). Use concordant lacunae as evidence but check for independent loss vs inherited gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concordance of contents and order across MSS
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement in which works are present and the order in which they appear (e.g. F, B, C containing the same Archimedes and Eutocius works in the same order) supports common derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text lists the seven principal works (sphere & cylinder; measurement of a circle; conoids; spirals; equilibrium of planes; sand-reckoner; quadrature of the parabola) and notes identical ordering in F, B, C. Use identical content sequence as one axis of stemmatic comparison alongside readings and orthography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of standard completion marks (colophons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of the usual completion marks (e.g. τέλος) or colophon in a manuscript may indicate that the archetype’s ending was illegible or missing, affecting inferred relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: no word τέλος at the end of F suggests the archetype’s end was illegible. Record presence/absence of such marks as data when reconstructing stemma and copying history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with contemporary translations and external testimonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence between readings in a manuscript and contemporary translators' quotations or translations (e.g. Valla’s translations agreeing with F) supports the manuscript’s text-type and dating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Valla’s translations largely agree with F; a 1491 letter by Angelus Politianus reporting a MS at Venice supports dating of F to ~1491. Similarly, a Latin translation sharing the same lacuna suggests it drew on the same MS. Use letters, printed prefaces, and translator remarks as corroborative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paleographic features (letter-forms, age of script) as dating criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of letters and abbreviation styles can indicate the date of a copy (e.g. many letters in F are older than 15th century style), helping to decide which witness is closer to the archetype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from text: the form of most letters in F is older than the 15th century, supporting early origin. Systematically record script features and compare to dated hands to place manuscripts chronologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scribe fidelity inferred from error patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: If a manuscript preserves mistakes that correspond to readings in an earlier translator or are shared with the archetype, this can indicate high fidelity to its exemplar; conversely, corrected or altered readings can indicate later emendation by scribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copyist of F kept to the original as shown by mistakes matching Valla’s readings; B’s scribe made many alterations ‘not always with success.’ Use patterns of shared errors (not just shared correct readings) as strong stemmatic evidence (the lectio difficilior and shared slips test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyist interventions and editorializing by scribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribes may make deliberate alterations, corrections, or interpolations on their own authority; such interventions can reduce trustworthiness or create mixed texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer of B altered many readings on his own authority; Tartaglia often filled gaps or inserted interpolations from other Greek MSS. Note marginal notes stating copyist decisions and treat heavy emendation as suspect without independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginalia, corrections, and added readings as indicators of editorial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Marginal corrections, added Greek readings, or directions for the printer by later hands inform how the text was edited and printed (e.g. Regiomontanus added Greek readings and marginal corrections; Venatorius wrote directions and corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Regiomontanus noted corrections of the Latin and added Greek readings; Venatorius corrected many mistakes and sometimes wrote on slips used in printing. Track these interventions to distinguish authorial text, exemplar readings, and editorial emendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Latin translations to Greek exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a Latin translation derives from a Greek manuscript or from another Latin translation; identical lacunae or errors in translations and MSS suggest shared source(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jacobus Cremonensis’ Latin translation shares the same lacuna as F, B, C, suggesting the translator had the Valla MS or a copy. Tartaglia copied Gauricus’ translation faithfully, reproducing its errors. Evaluate translations both as witnesses to readings and as potential independent corruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of editorial collation and edition history
rubrics_metrics.description: An edition’s reliability depends on whether it is based on fresh collations of manuscripts, the quality of collation, and editorial practices; poor collation or careless press corrections reduce trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heiberg’s edition is described as definitive because of close collation; Torelli’s collation was ‘not well done’ and the edition was not properly corrected in press. Prefer editions that explicitly collate multiple MSS, document variant readings, and provide apparatus criticus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal cross-references to approximate chronology of treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use citations within and between treatises (references to propositions used in later works) to infer the approximate chronological sequence of an author's works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction gives an approximate order for Archimedes’ works by noting internal references and reuse of proved properties (e.g. Quadrature of the Parabola earlier than some works). Use such internal textual evidence alongside external dating to order composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectal and linguistic evidence for later alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss or retention of dialectal forms (e.g. Doric forms) and the presence of later interpolations indicate stages of textual alteration and redaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes wrote in the Doric dialect; in many extant books traces of the dialect have disappeared, and interpolators acquainted with Doric made additions. Track dialectal forms to detect interpolation or subsequent linguistic assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of lost works through later citations and cautious inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify lost or doubtful works ascribed to an author by examining later authors’ citations (e.g. Pappus, Simplicius) and by noting when attributions are speculative or unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists probable lost works (e.g. On balances, On centres of gravity) known via later testimony; treat such attributions as plausible but subject to scrutiny, and note when Latin/Arabic attributions are doubtful or contradicted by internal evidence.
